title: The missed session
note: Fictional patient. Doses and energies are quoted from the 2025 AHA guidelines (and the ERC where named) for recognition; your unit protocol, crash-cart stock and the attending nephrologist come first. Simulation success is an educational result, not a prediction of patient survival.

monitor.ecg: Peaked T waves, QRS slightly wide

intro: Mr. Eduardo Panganiban, 55, missed Saturday for a family wake in Batangas. At 6:10 a.m. he is weak with heavy legs. His ECG shows peaked T waves and a slightly wide QRS. The potassium result will take 45 minutes. You are the physician-on-duty.

n1.prompt: What do you do before the result?

choices.text: Start the order set now: IV calcium, insulin with glucose, monitor and pads; connect promptly.
choices.feedback: ECG changes do not wait for the laboratory: protect, shift, remove. Salbutamol if prescribed; call the attending.

choices.text: Wait for the potassium result before treating, so you do not give calcium or insulin he may not need.
choices.feedback: The ECG already shows potassium effects; waiting risks arrest.
choices.then: At 6:40 you start calcium and insulin and connect him.

choices.text: Connect him without drugs, since dialysis removes potassium faster than any medicine.
choices.feedback: Dialysis is definitive but takes time; calcium protects the heart now.
choices.then: You add calcium and insulin after connection.

n2.scene: His rhythm slows to 40 and widens; then he is unresponsive and pulseless. Slow wide organized complexes on the monitor.

choices.text: Cardiac arrest (PEA): compressions, blood decision, epinephrine as soon as feasible.
choices.feedback: Arrest comes first; potassium is the reversible cause. The circuit nurse stops fluid removal and makes the blood decision; potassium is the leading cause.

choices.text: Give more calcium first and wait for the potassium result before starting compressions.
choices.feedback: Without a pulse, only compressions move blood.

n3.scene: The team asks about potassium drugs during the arrest.

choices.text: The unit protocol, decided in advance, with no pause in compressions.
choices.feedback: Guidelines differ; the protocol chooses, written beforehand. AHA 2025 rates calcium, bicarbonate and insulin as of uncertain effectiveness and advises against inhaled beta-agonists; ERC 2025 gives 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride with 50 mmol bicarbonate through separate lines.

choices.text: Calcium and bicarbonate in the same line, back to back and quickly, so potassium falls before the next check.
choices.feedback: They precipitate in the line; use separate lines or flush between.
choices.then: The drug nurse flushes the line between them.

choices.text: Inhaled salbutamol through the bag-mask, since it shifts potassium into the cells within minutes.
choices.feedback: AHA 2025: inhaled beta-agonists are not recommended in hyperkalemic arrest.

n4.scene: After epinephrine and protocol treatment, he has a pulse at 72 with a pressure of 100/60. Potassium returns at 8.1 mmol/L.

choices.text: Post-ROSC care; repeat potassium and glucose; the attending decides where dialysis continues.
choices.feedback: Potassium rebounds; dialysis restarts only on the attending’s decision. Keep pads on; usually monitored, possibly after transfer.

choices.text: Reconnect him immediately at high blood flow, since the potassium is still high, and call later.
choices.feedback: Restarting in an unstable patient is the attending’s decision.
choices.then: The attending is called and plans monitored dialysis.

end.title: 9:00 a.m.
end.text: Mr. Panganiban is dialyzed under monitoring after transfer. The social worker and attending review why he missed his session and plan for the next family event.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Treat ECG changes without waiting for the laboratory.
  • In arrest, CPR first; AHA and ERC differ on potassium drugs; the protocol decides.
  • Calcium and bicarbonate never share a line without a flush.
  • After ROSC, potassium rebounds; the attending decides on dialysis.
